Impacts

A global average hides the places that are changing fastest. GQ Atlas, by The Sonic Waves, is built so you can read that difference yourself, starting from NASA GISTEMP v4, the surface temperature record from NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies.

The same planet, uneven change

GISTEMP combines land and ocean observations into one map of how much warmer or cooler each area is than its own 1951–1980 average. On that map, the high latitudes stand out. The Arctic has warmed faster than the rest of the planet, a pattern called Arctic amplification. Open the atlas, choose surface temperature, and compare the Canadian Arctic with a mid-latitude city. The two cells share the same dataset, the same year, and the same baseline rule. The gap between them is the disproportionate part.

Land also tends to warm faster than the ocean beside it. A coastal city and a place a few hundred kilometres inland can tell different stories in the same year. That is why a single headline number, “the world is 1.2 °C warmer,” is a true summary and a poor description of any one home.

The atlas does not invent those gaps. Each cell is the grid square that contains the place you picked, about 2° on a side for GISTEMP. A city name is a label for that square, not a weather station on a street corner.

What that does to environments

Faster warming in the Arctic shortens the season of sea ice. Ice is a habitat: seals, polar bears, and the people who hunt and travel on the ice lose months of a surface that used to be reliable. The atlas sea-ice layer is NOAA’s OISST concentration, not a NASA product. Use it next to the GISTEMP temperature map so you can see warmth and ice loss as two records of the same region, and keep the sources straight.

On land, heat and water move together. A hotter surface dries soil faster, stresses crops, and raises the chance of fire weather. Extra rain does not always help: when it falls in fewer, heavier bursts, fields flood and then dry out. Precipitation, water vapor, and soil moisture in the atlas come from NOAA analyses. They show the local pattern. They do not, by themselves, prove a cause.

Oceans take up most of the extra heat. That heat shifts where fish can live, and warmer surface water adds stress to coral reefs. The sea-surface layer is NOAA ERSST. Read it as the ocean’s own anomaly, then compare a reef latitude with a high-latitude ocean cell if you want to see how uneven the surface warming is.

People feel this in the same uneven way. Communities that already live with thin ice, hot seasons, or unreliable rain have less slack. A year that is “a bit warm” on a global chart can be a failed hunt, a failed harvest, or a heat wave in a city with little shade. The atlas is a way to put a number on that local departure, including whether the 30-year trend at that cell is distinguishable from no change.

What you can do

Start with a comparison you can check. Pick your city and a place that is changing faster, such as the Arctic or a hot inland region. Read this year’s anomaly, the trend per decade, and the note on whether that trend is significant at 5%. If you cannot explain the difference in one sentence, the chart is doing its job: it is asking you to look again. The projections page says what the violet years are, and what they are not. They continue the recent line. They are not a forecast of future emissions.

The cuts that matter are the ones that reduce heat-trapping gases: using less fossil energy at home, supporting local transit and efficient buildings, and backing policies that do that at the scale of a city or a country. Local work still counts on its own terms. Shade, cool roofs, and checked-on neighbors reduce harm from heat that is already here. Farmers and northern communities need seasonal information more than a global slogan. Bring them the cell’s record, not a screenshot of a world average.

Share the comparison. A link to two places on the same map is easier to argue with than a slogan, and arguing with the data is the point. Methods, baselines, and the original files are on Data & methods. NASA GISTEMP is the temperature backbone. Say so when you cite a temperature map, and name NOAA when you cite rain, ice, or the reanalysis layers.
